lead: No natural product has grade A evidence in migraine, but several have randomized trials. A 2026 meta-analysis of 9 trials in 788 people found fewer headache days with melatonin than placebo, and meta-analyses of magnesium, riboflavin and coenzyme Q10 report fewer or shorter attacks, with mixed or low-certainty results (all grade B). Butterbur reduced attacks in two trials but has reports of serious liver injury.

grade_key.A: Meta-analysis, or at least 2 randomized trials with low risk of bias and a consistent benefit
grade_key.B: 1 good randomized trial, or several randomized trials with mixed results
grade_key.C: Observational studies, small pilots or open-label trials only
grade_key.Negative: Randomized trials found no benefit over placebo

disclaimer: This page summarizes published research. It is not medical advice. Talk to a clinician before starting any supplement, especially if you take other medicines.

products.name: Butterbur
products.summary: Two placebo-controlled trials tested a butterbur root extract. In a 4-month trial in 245 people, attacks fell by 48% at the higher dose tested (75 mg twice daily), against 26% with placebo; the lower dose was not better than placebo. A 12-week trial in 60 people also reported fewer attacks than placebo. A systematic review of both trials rated the evidence moderate and called for more studies of long-term safety.
products.safety_interactions: The 245-person trial reported mild stomach upset, mainly burping, and the 60-person trial reported no adverse events. The butterbur plant contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which a review describes as toxic and which make alkaloid-free extracts important. Spontaneous reports of liver injury have been collected for a defined butterbur root extract: nine people had severe liver injury and two needed a liver transplant, though the authors judged such cases rare and often confounded by other medicines. Reviews flag concern for hepatotoxicity. Speak to a clinician before using butterbur.

products.name: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10)
products.summary: A 2021 meta-analysis of 6 studies with 371 adults found shorter and less frequent migraine attacks with CoQ10 but no reduction in severity. A 2020 meta-analysis of 4 randomized trials with 221 people found about 1.9 fewer attacks a month, with no effect on severity or duration. A 2019 meta-analysis that pooled only 2 trials, with 97 adults, found no significant reduction in frequency.
products.safety_interactions: No safety data found in the cited trials.

general_safety.name: Coenzyme Q10
general_safety.short: Few adverse events were reported in trials. A case report describes reduced warfarin response while taking CoQ10.

products.name: Feverfew
products.summary: A Cochrane review found 6 placebo-controlled trials with 561 people. The largest, in 218 people, found 0.6 fewer attacks a month with feverfew than with placebo; three small trials were positive, and two rigorous trials found no difference. The reviewers rated the evidence low quality. In one of those trials, of 147 people, feverfew did not reduce attacks overall, only in a small predefined subgroup.
products.safety_interactions: The Cochrane review found only mild and transient adverse events, most often gastrointestinal complaints and mouth ulcers. In the 147-person trial, adverse events were similar with feverfew and placebo. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Feverfew
general_safety.short: Trials report only mild, transient effects (mainly stomach upset and mouth ulcers). One case report linked it to bleeding. Human pregnancy safety is unstudied.

products.name: Ginger
products.summary: For prevention, a 3-month placebo-controlled trial in 107 people found no benefit of ginger extract. For acute attacks, a trial in 60 people in an emergency room found better pain response at 1 to 2 hours when ginger was added to an intravenous painkiller, and a trial in 100 people found ginger powder comparable to sumatriptan. A 2026 meta-analysis of 8 trials with 594 people rated the certainty of evidence low to very low and concluded it is too uncertain whether ginger is effective.
products.safety_interactions: A 2021 meta-analysis of 3 trials found no difference in total adverse events between ginger and control, with less nausea and vomiting with ginger. In the sumatriptan comparison, ginger had fewer side effects. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Ginger
general_safety.short: Pregnancy trials found no significant rise in miscarriage (with wide uncertainty), heartburn or drowsiness. A warfarin review flags possible added bleeding risk.

products.name: Magnesium
products.route_note: oral for prevention; intravenous for acute attacks
products.summary: A 2016 meta-analysis of 21 randomized trials found that oral magnesium was linked to fewer and less intense migraine attacks and that intravenous magnesium relieved acute attacks, though some included trials did not use adequate randomization. A 2019 meta-analysis of 3 trials in 226 adults found no significant drop in migraine severity with oral magnesium (low strength of evidence). A 2014 meta-analysis of 5 randomized trials found no benefit of intravenous magnesium for acute pain relief.
products.safety_interactions: In the 2014 meta-analysis of intravenous magnesium for acute attacks, people given magnesium were significantly more likely to report side effects than controls. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Magnesium
general_safety.short: Oral magnesium mainly causes gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhoea; severe high blood magnesium occurs almost only in people with substantially reduced kidney function.

products.name: Melatonin
products.summary: A 2026 meta-analysis of 9 randomized trials in 788 people found fewer headache days, shorter and less severe attacks, and more responders with melatonin than with placebo; the antidepressant amitriptyline was generally more effective for attack duration and severity. In one trial, 196 people were randomized to melatonin 3 mg, amitriptyline or placebo for 12 weeks; migraine days fell by 2.7 with melatonin and 1.1 with placebo.
products.safety_interactions: In the meta-analysis, melatonin caused less sleepiness than amitriptyline, and the authors described a favourable safety profile. In the 12-week trial, melatonin was better tolerated than amitriptyline. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Melatonin
general_safety.short: Trial adverse events were few and mostly mild (daytime sleepiness, headache, dizziness); long-term data are limited. Drugs acting on CYP1A2 may slow its breakdown.

products.name: Riboflavin (vitamin B2)
products.summary: A 2022 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials and 1 controlled trial, with 673 people, found fewer migraine days, shorter and less frequent attacks and lower pain scores with riboflavin, and concluded that 400 mg a day for three months had a significant effect. Results varied a lot between trials for migraine days and pain. A 2017 systematic review of 11 trials described consistent benefit in adults but mixed results in children and adolescents.
products.safety_interactions: The 2017 systematic review reported that adverse reactions with riboflavin were generally mild. Interactions with medicines were not reported in the cited studies.

general_safety.name: Riboflavin (vitamin B2)
general_safety.short: Reviews describe riboflavin as unlikely to cause toxicity because excess is quickly eliminated; adverse events in migraine use are described as minimal.
